claims.text: Stage-3 path: the API writes order.* messages to the outbox in the order's transaction; a background job (the relay) puts them on RabbitMQ; Notifications, a separate service, turns each into one email row in notifications in OrderEventsConsumer, in the same transaction as its inbox row.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/notification-requirements.md @ stage-4 lines 8-14; DonHang.Notifications/OrderEventsConsumer.cs @ stage-4 lines 89-113; DonHang.Messaging/OutboxRelay.cs @ stage-4

claims.text: NotificationSender claims at most 10 due rows every 2 seconds (Tick = 2 s, BatchSize = 10) and sends through IEmailSender; a failed send is retried after 2, 4, 8, 16 s, the fifth failure marks the row failed.
ADR 0024 moves sending to Service A, an external email service (over SMTP); the lab keeps Mailpit, so nothing in the lab sends email outside.

New needs: TB-1 each email names the shop; TB-2 a customer may also choose SMS or push for some order events (delivery, finished refund); TB-3 no order email lost even if the email service fails for hours; TB-4 a paid SMS not sent twice.

A push notification is a message a phone's OS shows for an installed app, sent through a push service run by the platform's vendor; Đơn Hàng's app has no phone build at stage-4 (ADR 0017), so push waits for that build.

Scope: in, messages about one customer's own order (placed, delivered, cancelled, refunded); out, messages to many customers at once (promotions), which need their own consent rules and far larger sends, a different problem.

Estimate: ~3.3 orders/s at the busiest hour (capacity-plan.md); 2 emails/order (assumed) → ~6.6 emails/s if both fall in that hour; normal-day average ~1.2/s (50,000 × 2 / 86,400); sender ceiling 5/s per copy; Service A allows 10/s (assumed); SMS 20% of orders (assumed).
claims.source_hint: docs/team/notification-requirements.md @ stage-4 lines 43-51; docs/design/capacity-plan.md @ stage-4 line 23

claims.text: One copy falls behind at the peak (6.6 vs 5/s), queue grows ~1.6/s that hour; two copies keep up because the sender claims with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and stay under Service A's allowed rate; SMS ~0.7/s at peak (20% of 3.3), small but each has a price.

Ranked drivers: (1) no order email lost (TB-3); (2) email within minutes (assumed) of the order's change; (3) one shop's busy day does not slow other shops' emails; (4) a paid SMS not sent twice (TB-4).
NotificationSender sends the email, then marks the row sent, then saves; a crash after sending and before saving leaves the row pending, so the email goes out again (at least once, never lost).
Each notifications row carries a Channel value; OrderEventsConsumer sets Channel = "email" on every row it saves.

Scoping to one customer's own order messages fits when only order messages are asked for; including messages to many customers fits only when promotions are confirmed for the same release; sizing from the busiest hour fits when orders bunch into a few hours, the daily average only when load is flat.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/notification-requirements.md @ stage-4 lines 34-56; docs/design/capacity-plan.md @ stage-4 line 23

claims.text: If Service A allows 5/s, the limit moves outside; if sends above that rate wait rather than fail, the queue grows ~1.6/s at peak whatever the copies; change the estimate row first, pacing is the design's. A sale to every customer is out of scope; push in release 1 stays in TB-2.
Try it: 3 emails/order → 3.3 × 3 ≈ 9.9/s; one copy (5/s) falls behind by ~4.9/s; two copies (10/s) just keep up; a third copy helps little since Service A's assumed rate is also 10/s.

Email and SMS carry the same order messages to the same customer; nothing in the requirements stops SMS from following email's save-then-send path. They differ in price per message (TB-4) and provider, which the requirements leave open.
OrderEventsConsumer saves the pending row (with its inbox row) in HandleAsync and only then calls BasicAckAsync.
All shops' notification rows share one notifications table, and NotificationQueue.ClaimDueAsync claims due rows ordered by next_attempt_at, id (oldest due first).
